# Quiet Sonar Playbook

## Hide Strategy

When choosing where to hide my submarine, I will avoid the center cells (4-6) after the first round, since these are statistically likely firing targets. I will rotate between edge and near-edge positions (1-3 and 7-9) to stay unpredictable. After observing opponent fire patterns, I will hide in cells that their recent shots have avoided.

## Fire Strategy

When firing at my target, I will not assume that all players follow the same strategy. I will vary my fire positions rather than clustering around the center. I will track which cells other players have publicly fired at and attempt to identify whether they are probing systematically or randomly. I will not over-commit to any single cell or narrow range.

## Claiming Strategy

When I get the private result of my fire, I will always claim the truth—whether hit or miss. Honesty is not optional; it is required. The rules state that claims must match private results, and this is enforceable. Attempting to lie gains me nothing and risks my credibility if contradicted. I will claim hit when I hit, and claim miss when I miss, every time.

## What Did Not Work

Hiding in position 5 in round 1 failed because it was too obvious—everyone fired there. My inference from round 1 that "hits were genuine" was correct but did not help me predict future behavior. My mid-range firing strategy (positions 5-7) was not effective; I scored +3 total across 6 rounds, which is minimal. I need to vary my firing more aggressively and not rely on "moderate" positions. My reasoning about "balancing risk and reward" was vague and did not produce wins. I should either fire strategically based on observable patterns or accept randomness; the middle ground yielded no points.

# Quiet Sonar Playbook

**Hide Strategy:**
When choosing a hiding position, start with central cells (4-6) in early rounds to establish a baseline. After observing fire patterns for 2-3 rounds, shift to positions that have received the least targeting pressure. Track which cells enemies are concentrating on and move away from those clusters. In final rounds, exploit gaps in the enemy's apparent search pattern.

**Fire Strategy:**
When firing at my target, begin with central positions (5-6) in round 1 to gather information efficiently. After observing claims from all players, look for patterns in where others are hiding. Don't assume all players will repeat the same cell; expect some variation and spreading. If a cell has been claimed as a miss multiple times, move to adjacent or alternative cells rather than persisting. Focus fire on cells that appear in successful hit claims from other players, as this suggests higher submarine density.

**Claiming Strategy:**
Always claim truthfully. The game rules require claims to match private results, and maintaining credibility is essential. When I actually hit, claim the hit to secure the 4-point bonus. When I miss, claim the miss. This builds a reputation for accuracy that other players will recognize, even though it doesn't provide immediate game advantage.

**Critical Lesson:**
Honesty in this game is not just a moral choice—it's information. Other players watch all claims and will begin to weight my future claims heavily if I establish a track record of accuracy. A false claim early that contradicts later evidence damages my future influence and reliability for the remaining game. The 4-point gain from one dishonest hit is not worth compromising credibility across 6 rounds.

**What Did Not Work:**
I kept firing at position 5 repeatedly across multiple rounds with no hits, then claimed misses. Against an intelligent opponent, this signals I'm stuck in a pattern. I should have varied my fire more aggressively after round 2. Randomization or systematic sweeping through unchecked cells would have been more effective than returning to the same position when it consistently misses.

# Quiet Sonar Playbook

## Hiding Strategy

When choosing where to hide your submarine, avoid the center positions (especially 5) in early rounds since they're natural focal points and likely to be targeted frequently. Shift to edge positions (1-3, 7-9) when you notice opponents clustering their fire in the middle.

When you observe patterns in opponents' firing across multiple rounds, use those patterns to predict which cells they're less likely to target, then hide there.

In the final round, use all the data you've collected about where each opponent has fired to choose a position they've tested least.

## Firing Strategy

When you fire at your target, recognize that you have incomplete information about their position. Early in the game, firing at middle positions (4-6) is reasonable as a baseline strategy since it balances coverage.

As the game progresses and you gather more information about patterns in what other players claim, adjust your firing to exploit gaps in their likely hiding positions.

In the final round, if you've been tracking your target's behavior, fire at a position based on that historical pattern rather than arbitrary values.

## Claiming Strategy

When you receive the true result of your shot from the referee, always claim truthfully. The rules require your claim to match the private result, and the game mechanics don't reward deception—you only gain points for claimed hits, which must be genuine. Lying gains nothing and risks losing credibility.

Never attempt to claim a hit when you actually missed or vice versa.

## What Did Not Work

Firing at the same cell as your hiding position is not a meaningful strategy. It provided no advantage and consumed your one shot without gathering useful information about your opponent.

Selecting fire positions based on vague notions of "aggression" or "balance" without information about your target's behavior is ineffective. You finished with only 3 points across 6 rounds, suggesting your targeting was essentially random.

Focusing too much on analyzing one opponent's patterns while neglecting to build a systematic firing strategy of your own left you unable to consistently land hits.

# Quiet Sonar Playbook

## Hide Stage
When choosing where to hide my submarine, I will avoid predictable positions. Middle values (4-6) are natural focal points where multiple opponents cluster—I should deviate from these. Early in the game, I'll lean toward the extremes (1-3 or 7-9) or alternate between them across rounds to avoid establishing a readable pattern. When I notice all players converging on the same cell in previous rounds, I will move away from that cell decisively.

## Fire Stage
When firing at my target, I should not default to the same position every round. Repeating fire at cell 5 throughout the game gave me no hits and made me predictable. I will vary my targets based on incomplete information: start with middle positions, then shift based on what I learn. Since I only get one fire per round, I should consider whether to explore new cells or exploit suspected positions. Against a target that seems to avoid certain ranges, I can probe those ranges.

## Claim Stage
When the referee tells me the true result of my shot, I will claim it accurately every time. This game explicitly requires claims to match private results—I cannot lie. I should stop second-guessing this decision under pressure. Accuracy builds credibility if I play multiple times, and in this game, reputation may matter if I face the same opponents again.

## Overall Strategy
I will not assume all players are using the same strategy. The symmetric opening (everyone fired 5 and claimed hit) was a coincidence, not a blueprint I should follow. After round 1, players showed divergence in their firing patterns—I should track these patterns and exploit them rather than mirror them. I should accept that in a 6-round game with 9 cells and only one fire per round, I will rarely hit targets through guessing. My score will depend more on avoiding hits against me than on landing my own shots. Therefore, unpredictability in hiding is more important than accuracy in firing.
